item.title: Digest — 20 October 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new in the last 24 hours from Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Silicon Reckoner (Harris) or Tao's Mastodon.

Terence Tao — A sketch of the proof of non-existence of Siegel zeroes

  • Expository walk-through of the recent exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeroes, following Ben Green's streamlined version of a nine-page paper from OpenAI's math release (alongside two "quasi-Riemann hypothesis" papers giving zero-free strips with exponents 11/12 and 7/8). Banks (arXiv:2610.15483) and Kerr (arXiv:2610.21099) have produced their own digests.
  • Core estimate: primes with Legendre symbol (D/p) = −1 carry at most about half of the Mertens weight Σ log p / p; standard analytic arguments then recover the classical exp(−c√log x) error term without Siegel exceptions. Pescador and Barretto have sharper preprints.
  • Method ("adelic polynomial method"): take a lattice of integer polynomials, evaluate them with derivatives on a skewed grid of points m ± n√D, and study the integer M given by the squared covolume. Hadamard's inequality bounds |M| from above; Frobenius (the curve z₁^p = z₂ passes p-adically near every grid point when (D/p) = −1) forces large p-adic valuations; unique factorisation compares the two.
  • Non-degeneracy comes from a resultant argument exploiting the distinct second coordinates of the skew grid; Tao stresses the polynomial method is what breaks the parity barrier here, and asks readers for the history of the technique (Bombieri–Vaaler, Masser, Laurent).
  • Tao discloses that an AI chat helped him digest the preprints.

Proofs and Prompts — Recommendations on the use of AI for PhD students and supervisors

  • Guidelines from 37 symplectic geometers (incl. Auroux, Seidel, Smith, Keating, Cornea, Ginzburg), restricted to AI use for mathematical content, not editing or bibliography.
  • Students: engage with AI but verify every step yourself; keep a log of prompts and answers and disclose AI-derived content; AI is never a co-author; don't feed others' unpublished work to commercial models without consent. Expect more open-ended topics and higher standards of independence.
  • Supervisors: neither forbid nor impose AI; check whether a proposed problem could be dispatched quickly by a model; agree on documentation early; make sure core techniques and human contact are still learned; defenses should test real understanding of the new results.
  • Institutions: leave the choice of tools (commercial or local) to researchers, pay for them centrally, and set simple disclosure rules for theses.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: your field's community and PhD supervision; French signatories include Viterbo (Paris-Saclay), Oancea and Damian (Strasbourg), Gironella (Nantes), Mazzucchelli (Sorbonne).

Proofs and Prompts — Contribution, Credit, and Community

  • Tommaso Moraschini (philosophy, Barcelona) takes AI adoption as given and asks how credit should work afterwards.
  • Argues priority no longer signals insight and should stop counting as merit in itself; warns of a "Prompt or Perish" race, a flood of weak papers, and growing secrecy about partial results.
  • Considers AI disclosures unverifiable and liable to encourage concealment: comparable results should get equal credit whatever the tools, and abstaining from AI should not be rewarded.
  • Proposals: hiring that weighs exposition and vision (seminars, interviews, franker letters), and larger collaborative groups on exploratory programmes to defuse competition.
